Zakynthos Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Zakinthos, Greece

Not demolished. Jewish presence on Zakynthos dates to the late 15th century; Spanish and Portuguese expulsion (1492-97) refugees joined a small existing Romaniot community, though Venetian rulers required Jews to wear a yellow ribbon and hat. Population reached 30 families by 1522, peaking around 1,000 in 1686; the community was active in redeeming captives and lived in a ghetto while maintaining relations with Christian residents. An 1728 epidemic killed many, deepening community poverty; population reached 274 by 1811, with full citizenship granted following Greece's 1864 annexation, though antisemitism and poverty persisted. Earthquakes in 1893 and 1912 caused further deaths and damage. Population reached 275 (of 41,165 total) by 1940. Remarkably, Zakynthos's Jews were the only community in occupied Greece to survive destruction entirely, thanks to Mayor Lucas Karrer and Archbishop Demetrios Chrysostomos, both later named Righteous Among the Nations in 1978. Seventy Jews returned postwar, though most later emigrated. This cemetery's founding is unknown, likely 15th-16th century.
